learn.hook: A car's dashboard tells the driver if speed, fuel or engine heat drifts from normal. Controlling is a manager's dashboard.
points: Controlling means ensuring that activities in an organisation are performed as per the plans. It involves comparing actual performance with standards and taking corrective action.
It is a goal-oriented and pervasive function (needed at all levels and in all organisations).
Controlling is both backward-looking (it checks past performance, like a post-mortem) and forward-looking (it improves future performance by correcting deviations).

Importance: accomplishing organisational goals; judging the accuracy of standards; making efficient use of resources; improving employee motivation (employees know in advance on what basis they will be judged); ensuring order and discipline; facilitating coordination in action (all departments work to predetermined standards).

example.q: Comet Ltd found its standard of 200 calls per salesperson per day was always exceeded easily, so it raised the standard to 240. Which importance of controlling is shown?
steps: Comparing actual results showed the standard was too low.
This shows controlling helps in judging the accuracy of standards.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways tracks train punctuality daily against timetables and acts on delays, a clear example of controlling.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If the plan is good, why check anything afterwards?'
teach.praise: Even good plans drift! Controlling compares actual with standards and corrects the course.
teach.nudge: What does controlling compare, and what does it do when things go off track?

learn.hook: You can count units produced, but how do you measure employee morale or customer goodwill in numbers? Controlling has limits.
points: Difficulty in setting quantitative standards: it is hard to set measurable standards for things like employee morale, job satisfaction and human behaviour, so controlling becomes less effective there.
Little control over external factors: a firm cannot control government policy, technological changes or competition.
Resistance from employees: employees may see control as a restriction on their freedom, e.g. resisting CCTV surveillance.
Costly affair: controlling involves a lot of money, time and effort; small firms may not afford elaborate systems. Benefits should exceed costs.

example.q: Fine Fabrics installs cameras to monitor workers; workers protest that it invades their privacy. Which limitation of controlling is this?
steps: Workers see the cameras as a restriction on their freedom.

learn.reallife: A small kirana store cannot afford costly inventory software that a big retail chain uses: controlling is a costly affair.

games.title: Match the limitation

quiz.q: It is difficult to measure job satisfaction and employee morale in numbers. This limitation is:
quiz.explain: Human behaviour is hard to quantify.

quiz.q: A company cannot control a sudden change in technology or competition. Which limitation is this?
quiz.explain: External factors lie outside management's control.

quiz.q: Employees protesting against strict monitoring shows the limitation of:
quiz.explain: Employees may see control as limiting their freedom.
quiz.mistake: Thinks this is a cost issue

quiz.q: For a small firm, a sophisticated control system may not be justified because:

quiz.explain: Benefits must exceed the high cost of control.

options: It helps in judging the accuracy of standards

quiz.explain: Government policy is an external factor.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false because controlling is costly; R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can a manager control absolutely everything?'
teach.praise: No! Some things can't be measured, outside forces can't be controlled, people resist, and it costs a lot.
teach.nudge: Think about things outside the firm, and about cost and people's reactions.

learn.hook: A school sets a target of 95% attendance, records actual attendance daily, and compares the two each week. That's the start of the controlling process.
points: Step 1 Setting performance standards: standards are criteria against which actual performance is measured. Quantitative standards: cost, output, revenue, time (e.g. produce 1,000 units a day). Qualitative standards: goodwill, motivation, improving customer satisfaction.
Standards should be flexible enough to be modified when required.

Step 2 Measurement of actual performance: performance should be measured objectively and reliably, through personal observation, sample checking or performance reports. Measurement should be in the same units as the standard.

Step 3 Comparing actual performance with standards: reveals the deviation, i.e. the gap between actual and desired results. Deviation = actual − standard; percentage deviation = (deviation ÷ standard) × 100.

example.q: Standard output is 800 units a week. Actual output is 760 units. Find the deviation and the percentage deviation.

learn.reallife: Airlines in India set on-time performance standards and publish actual figures; comparing the two reveals deviations for corrective action.

quiz.explain: Standards must exist before performance can be judged.

quiz.explain: Shortfall = standard − actual.

quiz.explain: Divide the shortfall by the standard, not by the actual.

options: Deviations between actual and desired results
quiz.explain: Comparison shows gaps, which are deviations.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Since conditions change, standards must be adjustable. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I know if my flying practice is going well?'
teach.praise: Set a standard, measure my actual flight, and compare. Then I'll know my deviation!
teach.nudge: What must you set first, and what do you compare it with?

topics.title: Analysing deviations and taking corrective action

learn.hook: If postage costs rise 15% but labour costs rise 5%, which should worry the manager more? Critical point control gives the answer.
points: Step 4 Analysing deviations: deviations within an acceptable range need no action; significant deviations must be studied for their causes.
Critical point control: managers should focus on key result areas (KRAs) that are critical to success, e.g. a 5% rise in labour cost may matter more than a 15% rise in postal charges.
Management by exception: 'an attempt to control everything results in controlling nothing'. Only significant deviations beyond the permissible limit should be brought to the notice of management.

Step 5 Taking corrective action: e.g. defective material → change quality specifications; defective machinery → repair or replace; obsolete machinery → technology upgrade; defective process → modify the process; poor physical conditions → improve them; ineffective training → modify training; ineffective supervision → change supervision; lack of motivation → introduce new incentives.
If deviations cannot be corrected through managerial action, the standards may have to be revised.

example.q: Planned production cost is ₹50 per unit with a permissible deviation of 2%. Actual cost is ₹52. Should it be reported under management by exception?
steps: 4% exceeds the 2% limit, so it is significant and should be reported to management
example.answer: Yes, the 4% deviation exceeds the 2% limit

learn.reallife: A hospital such as AIIMS tracks critical indicators like infection rates closely while allowing minor variations in less critical areas: critical point control in practice.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If something goes slightly wrong, must the big boss know every time?'
teach.praise: Only big deviations go up the chain, and key areas get extra watch. Then fix the cause!
teach.nudge: Think about which deviations really need the boss's attention.

learn.hook: Planning without controlling is like setting a GPS destination and never checking the route. Controlling without planning is like checking a route that doesn't exist.
points: Planning and controlling are inseparable twins of management. Planning is the base for controlling, and controlling completes the planning cycle.
Planning without controlling is meaningless, and controlling without planning is blind: without plans there are no standards to control against.
Planning is prescriptive (it prescribes actions), while controlling is evaluative (it evaluates whether decisions were translated into action).

It is usually said that planning is looking ahead and controlling is looking back. But both are actually forward- and backward-looking: planning uses past experience (looking back), and controlling's corrective action improves future performance (looking forward).
Controlling also helps improve future planning by providing information from past performance.

example.q: A firm made a detailed sales plan but never checked actual sales. What is wrong, using the twins idea?
steps: Planning sets targets, but without controlling no one knows whether they are met.
So planning without controlling is meaningless.

learn.reallife: The Indian cricket team's analysts plan match strategies and then review match data to fine-tune the next plan, showing planning and controlling feeding each other.

Controlling is a prerequisite for planning

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Planning is only forward-looking and controlling is only backward-looking. Reason (R): Planning and controlling are both backward-looking as well as forward-looking.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false because both functions look in both directions; R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do people call planning and controlling twins?'
teach.praise: Plans give the standards, controlling checks them, and each improves the other. Perfect twins!
teach.nudge: What happens if you have a plan but never check it? Or check without a plan?
